title: Reasonable fees: Market evidence must match actual work
desc: Requires rate evidence tailored to practitioners and matters, separating field importance from complexity and AI reliability.

kps.k: The cluster concerns the evidentiary basis for reasonable legal fees, not a demonstrated finding about AI reliability.
kps.d: In the February 22, 2024 J.G. v. New York City Department of Education decision, the court awarded $53,050.13 against a $113,484.62 request despite the applicant’s success in two administrative proceedings. The supplied material supports analysis of market comparability, professional experience, reasonable hours and settlement consequences. Although the source heading highlights a ChatGPT-4 rate cross-check, the excerpts omit the underlying AI analysis; they do not establish that AI use caused the reduction or support a broader conclusion about AI-generated evidence.

qs.q: For the following  reasons, the Court grants the motion for fees and costs, but in an aggregate sum ($53,050.13)  below that sought.

kps.k: Market-rate evidence must match the work and practitioners at issue; broad surveys cannot substitute automatically for that inquiry.
kps.d: The court accepted the applicant’s contention that reasonable rates require case-specific evidence rather than exclusive reliance on previous awards. It nevertheless gave little weight to the submitted surveys and matrix. Its explained objections to the surveys concerned their aggregation of heterogeneous litigation practices rather than comparable Southern District of New York IDEA services. This was not a categorical rejection of survey evidence: suitable surveys can cross-check an award. Practically, applicants must connect comparators to the relevant practice, services, skill and experience.

qs.q: Instead, "the equation in the caselaw of a 'reasonable hourly fee' with the  'prevailing market rate' contemplates a case-specific inquiry into the prevailing market rates for  counsel of similar experience and skill to the fee applicants counsel," and it "requires an  evaluation of evidence proffered by the parties." kps.k: The court distinguished a field’s importance from case complexity and assessed compensation individually.
kps.d: The court recognized special education law’s importance and specialization but found no unusual novelty or complexity in this case. It reduced senior attorneys’ requested $550–$600 rates to $400. Yet it did not simply adopt DOE’s lower proposals: junior associate Erin Murray received $250 rather than DOE’s proposed $200 because her effective performance and the second proceeding’s procedural complexity warranted a rate toward the upper end of the junior range. Paralegal rates likewise reflected demonstrated experience, with the applicant bearing the burden of documenting qualifications.

qs.q: J.G., however, has not adduced any  evidence that this case presented novel or complex legal or factual issues relative to the typical  single-plaintiff IDEA case.

kps.k: Recoverable fees depend on justified hours and statutory settlement consequences as well as hourly rates.
kps.d: The firm billed 226.4 hours for the administrative proceedings and 50.5 hours for the fee litigation. The court agreed with DOE that hours at both stages were excessive, although the supplied excerpts do not quantify the reductions. Separately, J.G. rejected DOE’s $54,300 settlement offer of May 26, 2023. Because reasonable fees and costs through that date fell below the offer, the court excluded later accruals. The practical implication is that applicants must substantiate time spent and assess settlement offers against likely recoverable fees, not merely their billed totals.

qs.q: Administrative Proceedings          In various respects, the Court finds excessive or inadequately explained the hours on  which the Cuddy Law Firm bases its fee request.

vlens.an: This court source directly supports the proposition that reasonable-fee determinations require evidence matched to the actual legal work and the professionals performing it. Its central reasoning favours a case-specific inquiry into comparable practice area, market, skill and experience, while rejecting aggregated rate data that obscures those factors. It also assesses complexity separately from the importance of special-education work, differentiates rates by individual experience and performance, scrutinises whether billed hours were justified, and applies the statutory consequence of rejecting a settlement offer. The source contains some internal qualification but no substantive disagreement: surveys are not categorically excluded and may serve as a cross-check when suitably comparable. Nor do the supplied excerpts substantiate a finding about AI reliability, so the source supports the proposition’s evidentiary caution on that issue. Because this facet contains one curated court source, the conclusion describes that source rather than regulators, courts and professional bodies generally.

qs.q: Instead, "the equation in the caselaw of a 'reasonable hourly fee' with the  'prevailing market rate' contemplates a case-specific inquiry into the prevailing market rates for  counsel of similar experience and skill to the fee applicants counsel," and it "requires an  evaluation of evidence proffered by the parties." elens.an: The sole curated source for the 2023–2024 period directly supports the proposition that reasonable legal fees must rest on evidence matched to the actual matter and practitioners. The J.G. ruling requires a case-specific inquiry into rates for counsel with comparable skill and experience, and rejects broad aggregated statistics as an automatic proxy where they combine unlike practice areas and services. Its support is qualified rather than absolute: suitable survey evidence may still serve as a cross-check, and compensation is assessed individually by experience and performance. The court also separates the importance of special-education law from the demonstrated complexity of this particular case, while treating justified hours and the consequences of a rejected settlement offer as independent constraints on recovery. Although the source’s heading refers to a ChatGPT-4 cross-check, the supplied excerpts contain no underlying AI analysis, so this evidence supports no broader conclusion about AI reliability or causation.
